html:
The Kalyan Minaret is a tall brick tower in the centre of Bukhara, in Uzbekistan, built in 1127 by the Kara-Khanid ruler Arslan Khan. It is about 46 metres high, and for centuries it was the tallest building in Central Asia.

Its tapering round shaft is covered in bands of baked brick laid in different patterns, with a band of blue glazed tile, one of the earliest uses of glazed tile in the region.

A famous story says that when Genghis Khan took Bukhara in 1220, he looked up at the tower so far that his hat fell off. He bent to pick it up and, struck by the building that had made him bow, ordered it spared. The rest of the city was largely destroyed in the Mongol invasion.

Today it stands at the heart of the Po-i-Kalyan complex, between the great Kalyan Mosque and the Mir-i-Arab madrasa, both from the 16th century. It continues the brick craft of the older Samanid Mausoleum, and is a close cousin of the Minaret of Jam.
